Veteran filmmaker Peter Medak passes away

Peter Medak, the Hungarian‑British director whose work spanned six decades of cinema and television, died peacefully on October 27, 2026 in Los Angeles at the age of 88. The announcement was made by his family, who chose not to disclose a cause of death. Medak’s career included cult classics such as The Changeling (1980) and Romeo Is Bleeding (1993), as well as acclaimed black comedies like The Ruling Class (1972).

---

Early life and emigration

Born on December 23, 1937 in Budapest, Medak’s fascination with film began at age eight when his aunt gave him a 35‑mm hand‑cranked projector and a strip of film. Under Hungary’s communist regime, he was barred from school at 13 after his father—labeled a “capitalist”—was imprisoned. Medak later recalled spending long hours alone in his apartment, observing life through a “keyhole” that sharpened his visual sensibility.

In 1956, at 18, he fled the Hungarian uprising and settled in England. He entered the British film industry as a trainee at Associated British‑Pathe, quickly moving up to assistant director on productions such as The Great Armored Car Swindle (1961) and The Phantom of the Opera (1962). His work caught the attention of MCA Universal Pictures, which brought him to Los Angeles in 1963 under a television‑directing contract.

---

Film and television milestones

Medak’s first feature, Negatives (1967), starred Glenda Jackson and marked his transition from television to cinema. The early 1970s proved pivotal: A Day in the Death of Joe Egg (1972) and The Ruling Class (1972) earned critical praise, the latter securing a Palme d’Or nomination at Cannes and an Academy Award nod for lead actor Peter O’Toole.

He earned a reputation as an “actors’ director,” collaborating with talents such as George C. Scott (The Changeling), Gary Oldman (Romeo Is Bleeding), and the Kemp brothers (The Krays, 1990). His filmography totals 27 feature films and 59 television episodes, including episodes of Homicide: Life on the Street, Chicago Hope, The Wire and Breaking Bad.

Beyond narrative film, Medak directed early music videos for Pink Floyd and Peter Gabriel, and staged operatic productions like La voix humaine with Julia Migenes, a production of Salome in Minneapolis, and Rigoletto for the Los Angeles Opera.

In 2018, his documentary The Ghost of Peter Sellers won Best Documentary at the Beverly Hills Film Festival, underscoring his continued relevance in the documentary arena.

---

Personal life and legacy

Medak was survived by four children—Christopher, Joshua, Karen and Cornelia—and five grandchildren. He had been married to Katherine La Kermance, actress Carolyn Seymour, and opera singer Julia Migenes, and was in a relationship with Christine Wagner at the time of his death.

Reflecting on his lifelong devotion to directing, Medak once said, “If it’s in your blood, directing. You never stop directing and it doesn’t matter that you’re alone in your mind, dreaming or imagining things but you’re always making a movie.”

---

Practical implications for the industry

  • Retrospectives and restorations – Film societies and streaming platforms are likely to schedule retrospectives of Medak’s work, especially The Changeling and The Ruling Class, which continue to influence horror and dark‑comedy genres.
  • Educational value – Film schools may incorporate his directing techniques, particularly his actor‑focused approach, into curricula on performance‑driven storytelling.
  • Archival interest – Medak’s early music‑video work and opera productions are relatively under‑documented; archivists may seek to preserve these pieces as part of a broader study of cross‑medium directing.
